title: Shear strength of laminates cured at two temperatures
intro:
A composites shop cures carbon-fiber laminates at two temperatures and tests the interlaminar shear strength (MPa) of coupons cut from separate panels. Cure 1: n₁ = 11 coupons, mean 62.4 MPa, standard deviation 3.1 MPa. Cure 2: n₂ = 9 coupons, mean 58.9 MPa, standard deviation 3.6 MPa. Both samples looked normal, and the variance ratio is 3.6²/3.1² = 1.35, so equal variances are reasonable. Test H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 against H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0 at α = 0.05 with the **pooled t-test**.

Find the t statistic, its degrees of freedom, the two-sided p-value, and the 95 % confidence interval for μ₁ − μ₂. Give t and the interval to two decimals, and p to three decimals or more.

To use the Workbench: press Ctrl+B and choose **Two-sample test**. Set **Test** to *Two means, equal variances (pooled t)*, **Data from** to *Summary statistics entered here*, **Alternative hypothesis** to *Two-sided (≠)*, **Significance level (α)** to 0.05 and **Hypothesised difference (Δ₀)** to 0, then type the means, standard deviations and sizes into the sample 1 and sample 2 boxes. Ctrl+L brings you back.

ask.prompt: 95 % CI for μ₁ − μ₂, lower end (MPa)
95 % CI for μ₁ − μ₂, upper end (MPa)

Statistic.says: That is Welch's t, with the variances kept apart. The exercise asks the pooled t: SE = sₚ √(1/n₁ + 1/n₂).

DegreesOfFreedom.says: n₁ + n₂ = 20. Each sample's standard deviation uses up one degree of freedom: the pooled test has n₁ + n₂ − 2.
That is Welch's ν. The pooled test has n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom.

PValue.says: That is a one-tailed p-value. H₁ is two-sided (≠), so p = 2 × P(T > |t|).
That is the p-value of Welch's test. The exercise asks the pooled test, with n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom.

CiLower.says: You used z = 1.96. With samples this small, use the t quantile with n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 18 degrees of freedom.

CiUpper.says: You used z = 1.96. With samples this small, use the t quantile with n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 18 degrees of freedom.

hints: First the pooled standard deviation: sₚ² = [(n₁ − 1)s₁² + (n₂ − 1)s₂²]/(n₁ + n₂ − 2).
SE = sₚ √(1/n₁ + 1/n₂) and t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/SE, with n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom.

p = 2 × P(T > |t|): Python 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), df), R 2 * pt(abs(t), df, lower.tail = FALSE). The interval is (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ± t(0.025, df) × SE, with t(0.025, df) from Python stats.t.ppf(0.975, df) or R qt(0.975, df).
